reference.source: Williams Hematology / WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours
clinicalPearls: A group of kidney disorders caused by a nephrotoxic monoclonal immunoglobulin produced by a B-cell or plasma-cell clone that is itself too small to meet criteria for myeloma or lymphoma
The clone would otherwise be labelled a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, but the renal damage reclassifies it as clinically significant
Patients present with proteinuria, haematuria, progressive renal impairment or nephrotic syndrome without another clear cause
The kidney lesions are diverse and include monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease, proliferative glomerulonephritis with monoclonal deposits, light chain proximal tubulopathy and AL amyloidosis
A renal biopsy with immunofluorescence and electron microscopy is central to demonstrating the monoclonal immunoglobulin in the kidney
The paraprotein detected in serum or urine must be shown to match the deposited immunoglobulin to establish causation
Treatment is directed against the underlying clone to remove the pathogenic protein and preserve kidney function, and disease can recur after transplantation if the clone persists
reference.pathophysiology: Monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance describes kidney injury caused by a monoclonal immunoglobulin or its fragments secreted by a small, non-malignant B-cell or plasma-cell clone. Despite a low tumour burden, the abnormal protein has physicochemical properties that make it nephrotoxic: it may deposit in glomerular or tubular basement membranes, form organised fibrils or crystals, aggregate within proximal tubular cells, or activate complement, depending on its structure. These mechanisms produce a spectrum of glomerular and tubulointerstitial lesions. Because damage stems from the protein rather than tumour bulk, effective treatment must suppress the clone that produces it.
additionalDifferentials: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance without renal disease
additionalInvestigations: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains
Renal biopsy with immunofluorescence and electron microscopy
Matching of the deposited immunoglobulin with the circulating paraprotein
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to characterise the clone
Quantification of proteinuria and assessment of renal function
Cross-sectional imaging or further staging to exclude overt myeloma or lymphoma
redFlags: Rapidly progressive renal impairment threatening dialysis dependence
Features suggesting systemic amyloidosis or evolving overt malignancy
Recurrence of disease in a kidney transplant
reference.prognosis: Kidney outcome depends on early recognition and effective clone-directed therapy; timely treatment can stabilise or improve renal function, whereas delayed diagnosis often leads to irreversible kidney failure, and the disease may recur after transplantation if the clone is not controlled.
pitfalls: Dismissing a small monoclonal protein as benign despite unexplained kidney disease
Not performing a renal biopsy to define the specific lesion
Failing to confirm that the renal deposits match the circulating paraprotein
Transplanting the kidney without controlling the underlying clone, risking recurrence
